name: Building Revision Into Class
title: Building Revision Into Class
answer: Building revision into class means making revision a planned, guided part of the lesson rather than an optional extra. Students draft, receive AI feedback, revise, discuss with peers, and reflect as a class while the teacher guides the process. It matters because it gives students a reason to act on feedback and shifts the teacher from writing every comment to steering the cycle.

sections.body: This idea addresses the problem that feedback often goes unused when it arrives as a comment on a finished piece of work. The proposed fix is a lesson model in which students draft, receive AI feedback, revise on their own, discuss their revisions with peers, and then reflect as a class with the teacher guiding. Each step in that sequence gives students a reason to engage with the feedback rather than ignore it. The teacher's role changes from writing every comment to guiding the process. Goal setting is added because a student who sets a specific goal, such as adding evidence to each paragraph, has a clear reason to revise.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, teachers build a short goal setting step into every revision cycle so students have a concrete aim when they revise. The cycle runs through drafting, AI feedback, independent revision, peer discussion of the revisions, and a class reflection led by the teacher. The text does not give separate grade band versions, but it describes the model generally and reports a study with upper secondary students learning English, where goal setting based on automated scores produced the largest gains in revision. Teachers should review AI feedback before students see it, at least until they know how a tool behaves, because a quick scan can catch errors, harsh wording, or feedback that misses the point. The text notes that AI feedback can misread English learners' writing, so unreviewed feedback can confuse or discourage students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea with research support. It cites a proposed model in which students draft, receive AI feedback, revise on their own, discuss their revisions with peers, and then reflect as a class with the teacher guiding (Helm & Hesse, 2026). It also cites a study with 345 upper secondary students learning English in which goal setting based on automated scores produced the largest gains in revision (Jansen et al., 2024). The text further reports that AI feedback can misread English learners' writing, which is presented as a reason for teacher review rather than as a separate study finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Teachers should review AI feedback before students see it, at least until they know how a tool behaves, because a quick scan can catch errors, harsh wording, or feedback that misses the point. Feedback released without review can confuse or discourage students, and the text notes that AI feedback can misread English learners' writing. The decisions that stay with a person are the teacher's review of the feedback and the teacher's guidance of the revision cycle, including the class reflection. The text does not describe legal duties or compliance rules, and nothing here is legal advice.
